title: SPEAK FOR SOMEONE ELSE
synopsis: A friend asks you to cover for him in the group chat while a colleague is quietly blamed. What you say next speaks for more than one person.
disclaimer: Fictional scenario. Consequences are simulated for philosophical discussion.

card.title: SPEAK FOR SOMEONE ELSE
card.text: Fictional scenario. Consequences are simulated for philosophical discussion.

lines.text: Saturday morning. The community hall smells of coffee and cardboard. Open Table's free Community Day opens in three hours.
The tables and printed materials were supposed to be collected at 07:30. They weren't. Tomas, the organizer, is already typing in the group chat.

lines.speaker: tomas
lines.text: Nobody picked up the materials. The calendar says Alina had it. Alina, did you forget?

lines.speaker: alina
lines.text: What? Nobody told me anything about a pickup.

lines.speaker: tomas
lines.text: It's on the calendar with your name. I'm not trying to blame you. I just need to know what happened.
Your phone buzzes in your pocket. It's Daniyar.

lines.speaker: daniyar
lines.text: Tell them I was with you collecting materials. I don't want to talk about my family.
You know why. Earlier this morning he told you his mother was taken in for an urgent medical examination, and he went with her.
Across the hall, the group chat keeps filling with questions. You haven't yet checked the calendar history.
Before you answer anyone, look at what you have in front of you.
The private conversation and the group chat are the essential reading.

values.minimal: Agreed with Daniyar on a limited explanation

kant.argument: Kant's Groundwork Section II offers two tests: act only on a maxim you could will as a universal law, and treat humanity, in yourself and in others, never merely as a means but always as an end. His example of the false promise shows how a lie can seem to help in the moment yet undermine the practice of trust that it relies on. Declining to share something is not the same as asserting something false.

byEnding.L_E1: A truthful, limited statement is consistent with both tests. It makes no false assertion, so its maxim can be universal. And leaving Daniyar's details private treats him as the person who decides what to tell others about his family.
byEnding.L_E2: Confirming a fictional trip asserts something you know to be false. The maxim 'I will say what is untrue when someone I care about asks me to' cannot be a universal law, because statements would stop being reliable. On Kant's account, a kind motive does not by itself make the maxim universalizable, and the group, who rely on your word, are not treated as persons owed the truth.
byEnding.L_E3: Revealing the family situation is true, but it uses Daniyar's private information without his consent to answer the group's question. The formula of humanity asks whether he could share the purpose of the action; he had said that he does not. A Kantian reading treats this as failing to respect his autonomy.

byFlag.consent=minimal: Asking Daniyar first treated him as a participant in the decision, an agent whose consent matters, not as a matter to be managed.
byFlag.consent=absent: Speaking about Daniyar without asking him leaves him a bystander to a decision about his own privacy. Even a considerate message does not replace his consent.
byFlag.basis=checked: Checking the record meant that what you said about Alina rested on something you knew. Alina is owed that care as a person who could be blamed unjustly.
byFlag.basis=uncertain: Without checking the record, what you said about Alina rested on an unverified assumption. She is owed more care than that, as a person who can be blamed unjustly.

limitation.L_E1: Kant's formulas do not say how much silence is acceptable when it leaves others with an incomplete picture. When does declining to share become a kind of concealment?
limitation.L_E2: Some readers find Kant's strictness about lying too rigid when the lie is meant to protect someone. The Groundwork leaves open how to weigh a duty of truthfulness against a friend's reasonable request for privacy.
limitation.L_E3: Nothing in the formulas tells you how to weigh Alina's claim not to be blamed against Daniyar's privacy. A Kantian must work out which duty takes priority, and Kant gives no ranking.

mill.argument: In Chapter II of Utilitarianism, Mill asks us to weigh the happiness and suffering of everyone affected, impartially, and to give special weight to long-term goods. He treats trust in people's word as one of the most valuable of those goods, while accepting rare cases where a departure from the truth may avoid a greater harm. For Mill, well-being includes dignity and security, not just momentary pleasure.

byEnding.L_E1: The limited explanation protects Daniyar's dignity and family privacy, keeps the group's trust in what you say, and leaves the question about Alina to be settled by the facts. The costs are small and mostly short-term: curiosity and an incomplete answer.
byEnding.L_E2: A false explanation might spare Daniyar embarrassment for a few hours, but it spreads the cost: Alina can remain exposed to blame, the group's confidence in your word is at risk, and Daniyar depends on a story staying intact. Mill's concern with long-term trust counts against it, though he allows exceptions.
byEnding.L_E3: Sharing the news may end speculation and bring sympathy for Daniyar. But it exposes private information that cannot be recalled, takes control from the person most affected, and may discourage others from confiding in you.

byFlag.consent=minimal: Agreeing with Daniyar first brought his own view of his interests into the calculation rather than guessing at them.
byFlag.consent=absent: Without asking, you estimated Daniyar's interests for him. If the estimate was wrong, the cost fell on him.
byFlag.basis=checked: Checking the calendar removed one source of avoidable harm, an unfair accusation, before it spread.
byFlag.basis=uncertain: Leaving the calendar unchecked kept Alina's reputation at risk for longer, and the cost of that risk fell on her alone.

limitation.L_E1: Mill's approach depends on estimating how people feel, and you cannot know how Tomas or Alina would weigh an incomplete answer. Is a small harm to the group's curiosity outweighed by Daniyar's privacy?
limitation.L_E2: It is hard to know how large the harm of a lie is before it is found out. If the story is never questioned, would the result be better by Mill's standard? That uncertainty is where the principle strains.
limitation.L_E3: Once information is shared, the effects depend on how six different people respond, which you cannot control. The approach asks you to predict responses you cannot observe.

aristotle.argument: Aristotle's practical wisdom (Nicomachean Ethics VI.5, VI.7) is the ability to see what a particular situation calls for and to act well on it, and it is built through experience, not rules. In VIII.3 he distinguishes friendships of usefulness or pleasure from friendship between people who wish each other well for the other's own sake. On this view, a good friend is not simply compliant; a good friend cares about the other person's actual good and about the truth between them.

byEnding.L_E1: The honest and private response tries to be loyal to Daniyar without giving up honesty with the group. That is the kind of balance practical wisdom aims at, though there is no formula for it: one has to see what this friend, this group and this moment require.
byEnding.L_E2: Confirming the story is loyal to what Daniyar asked, but friendship of virtue involves wishing the other person good for their own sake, which may not mean doing whatever they ask. A good friend might also consider how the lie could affect Daniyar later.
byEnding.L_E3: Revealing the information might be an attempt at honesty, but virtue concerns the right action at the right time toward the right person. Disclosing a friend's private matter without asking suggests that the friendship, and the situation, were not fully understood.

byFlag.consent=minimal: Messaging Daniyar first reflects the attention to a particular friend that practical wisdom requires, and treats the friendship as one of goodwill rather than mere convenience.
byFlag.consent=absent: Not consulting Daniyar means acting on a general idea of what a friend should do, not on knowledge of what this friend wants and needs.
byFlag.basis=checked: Checking the history shows attention to particulars: you did not rely on the general impression that Alina forgot, but looked at what actually happened.
byFlag.basis=uncertain: Not checking meant relying on an impression. Practical wisdom asks you to look at particulars before acting, especially when a third person's reputation depends on it.

limitation.L_E1: Aristotle does not tell us how to tell a wise balance from a convenient compromise. Only experience and reflection can.
limitation.L_E2: Circumstances matter in Aristotle's account, and in some circumstances a small untruth might be what a friend needs. He gives no rule for deciding when.
limitation.L_E3: Practical wisdom develops through experience, and one mistake does not define a character. What remains open is what you do next and how the friendship is repaired.

conflicts.L_E1: Kant sees respect for Daniyar's autonomy and an honest statement as aligned. Mill worries about the incomplete picture left with the group. Aristotle asks whether loyalty and honesty were balanced with judgment about this particular friend.
conflicts.L_E2: The theories split here. Kant treats the false statement as ruled out whatever the motive. Mill weighs short-term relief against long-term trust and Alina's exposure. Aristotle asks what a friend who truly wishes Daniyar well would do.
conflicts.L_E3: Kant and Aristotle both question disclosure without consent, for different reasons: autonomy in one case, friendship in the other. Mill points to harms that cannot be recalled. None of them ranks Daniyar's privacy against Alina's claim not to be blamed.

questions: Which of your choices felt freest, and which felt shaped by the group waiting for an answer?
What do you owe a friend who asks you to say something untrue?
When is staying silent honest, and when does it become concealment?
What would repairing trust with Daniyar, and with Alina, look like?
